answers.question: Actual SAR rates freelancers charge per Mostaql bookkeeping/invoice-entry gig (never disclosed in any listing found)
answers.answer: Direct per-gig prices on individual Mostaql project pages could not be fetched in this session (WebFetch to mostaql.com was blocked by the proxy). However, adjacent market-rate evidence was found: (1) multiple real Mostaql project listings exist for invoice/data-entry and bookkeeping tasks (e.g. daily purchase-invoice entry into Excel, converting invoice images to structured Excel data, entries into 'Daftra'/'Qoyod' accounting software), confirming real demand but not showing bid amounts in the search snippets. (2) Broader Saudi remote/independent bookkeeping service pricing (non-Mostaql) ranges from roughly SAR 1,500–4,000/month for SME bookkeeping, and one Monshaat-linked 'Mazaya' bookkeeping service package is listed at SAR 3,000 (SAR 2,250 after discount). These are monthly retainer prices for full bookkeeping, not per-gig Mostaql task prices, so they only proxy the willingness-to-pay ceiling, not the actual freelancer piece-rate for invoice entry.

answers.question: Real Arabic OCR accuracy achievable with LLM-vision APIs (Claude/GPT-4o) on messy/handwritten Saudi supplier invoices -- untested in this session
answers.answer: No direct test on real Saudi supplier invoices was run, but published benchmarks give a strong proxy. A cross-lingual handwritten-OCR benchmark found GPT-4o achieved a mean Arabic accuracy of 0.959 (best-trial 0.978) and Claude Sonnet 4 achieved 0.921 mean (best-trial 0.979) — i.e. high but not perfect, and this is on a curated handwriting benchmark, not messy real-world Saudi invoices with stamps/stains/mixed fonts, which typically perform worse. Separately, a vendor benchmark specifically on (printed, business) invoice-field extraction found Gemini ~94%, GPT+external OCR ~91%, Claude+external OCR ~90% accuracy — these are for structured Latin/mixed invoices, not messy handwritten Arabic. Conclusion: LLM-vision Arabic OCR is in the ~90-96% range on clean/benchmark data, but real messy handwritten Saudi invoices (stamps, cursive Arabic, poor scans) will likely score meaningfully lower and require human QA/correction workflow — this residual error rate is a genuine product-design constraint, not a solved problem.

answers.question: Whether customers would trust an unsupervised AI tool for VAT-sensitive reconciliation without a human-in-the-loop, which would raise the founder's operating cost/complexity
answers.answer: Evidence points to NO — the professional and vendor consensus is that AI should draft/pre-process while a qualified human reviews and finalizes VAT-relevant entries. Industry sources explicitly warn that fully automatic accounting without review risks misclassified transactions, missed tax/legal details, undetected biased outputs, and audit-trail/compliance gaps that create liability exposure; the recommended model is 'AI prepares, human reviews, accountant finalizes under professional supervision,' with VAT treatment and unusual transactions specifically flagged for accountant sign-off. In the Saudi/GCC market itself, existing ZATCA-compliance products lean toward giving accountants editable templates/dashboards (human-controlled) rather than fully autonomous reconciliation, and audit-prep guidance stresses that supporting invoices/ledgers must be manually verified to match records before ZATCA inspection. This implies a solo founder cannot sell a 'fully unsupervised' VAT reconciliation tool with confidence — the product will need a human-in-the-loop review/approval step (raising ops complexity: either the founder or the customer's accountant must review outputs), which should be priced/scoped into the MVP rather than promised away.
